questions.q: An Apollo capsule comes home from the Moon at a 6.5° entry angle with the autopilot. What is its peak braking force, and at what height?
questions.do: Set Capsule to Apollo command module, click The Moon, set Entry angle at 122 km to 6.50° and Steering to Autopilot: roll the lift to stay under 4 g. Read Peak braking and At altitude.
questions.a: About 6.6 g at about 57 km. That is under the 10 g crew limit this page uses, so the verdict says “Home”.

questions.q: Keep Apollo returning from the Moon with the autopilot. What happens at an entry angle of 3°, and at 12°?
questions.do: With Apollo command module, The Moon and the autopilot, move Entry angle at 122 km to 3.00° and read the verdict. Then move it to 12.00°.
questions.a: At 3° it skips out: too shallow, it bounces off the upper air. At 12° the braking hits about 38.9 g, far above the 10 g crew limit. The safe window lies in between.

questions.q: At 6.5° from the Moon, how much does steering with lift help? Compare the autopilot with no lift.
questions.do: Use Apollo command module, The Moon, 6.50°. Read Peak braking with Autopilot: roll the lift to stay under 4 g, then switch Steering to No lift (ballistic, like a Soyuz failure).
questions.a: Autopilot: about 6.6 g. No lift: about 15.3 g at 44 km, “Crew in danger”. Rolling the lift keeps the capsule higher in thin air for longer, so it slows down more gently.

questions.q: Why is it harder to come home from the Moon than from low orbit? Compare the width of the entry corridor.
questions.do: With Apollo command module and the autopilot, click The Moon and read the line under The corridor chart. Then click Low orbit and read it again.
questions.a: From the Moon (11.03 km/s) the corridor runs from about 5.75° to 7.00°, only 1.50° wide. From low orbit (7.8 km/s) it is about 5.50° wide. A faster capsule carries much more energy, so it skips out more easily when shallow and brakes too hard when steep. The window to hit is much narrower.

questions.q: Which capsule made the fastest return of any human-made object, and how hard did it brake?
questions.do: Set Capsule to Stardust sample capsule and read the note under it. Then read the Stardust rows in How far to trust it.
questions.a: Stardust, which brought comet dust home in 2006 at 12.9 km/s (46,440 km/h). It peaked at 34 g at 55 km. This model gets about 36.8 g at 54 km.
